topic: How vaccines train the immune system

concepts.name: Innate immunity
concepts.explanation: The fast, general first line of defence: barriers, inflammation and cells like neutrophils and macrophages that react to common danger signals.
concepts.caveat: Innate immunity is not "dumb"; it detects pathogen patterns and strongly shapes the adaptive response that follows.
concepts.question: Why would a vaccine that triggers no innate response often produce weak immunity?

concepts.name: Adaptive immunity
concepts.explanation: The slower, highly specific defence carried out by B and T cells, which learns particular targets and remembers them.
concepts.caveat: Adaptive does not mean it adapts to anything instantly; a first response takes days to weeks to build.
concepts.question: Why are you usually sick for several days the first time you meet a new virus?

concepts.name: Antigen
concepts.explanation: Any molecule, often a piece of a pathogen's protein, that B cells or T cells can specifically recognise.
concepts.caveat: Not every part of a pathogen makes a good target; some antigens mutate quickly or are hidden from antibodies.
concepts.question: Why do vaccine designers care which part of a virus they use as the antigen?

concepts.name: Antigen-presenting cell
concepts.explanation: Cells such as dendritic cells that capture antigens, carry them to lymph nodes and display them to T cells to start an adaptive response.
concepts.caveat: Presentation is not just showing; these cells also send signals that decide what kind of response follows.
concepts.question: What happens to a T cell that sees its antigen without the extra activating signals?

concepts.name: Helper T cell
concepts.explanation: CD4+ T cells that coordinate the response, helping B cells make strong antibodies and helping other immune cells act.
concepts.caveat: Helper T cells do not kill infected cells directly, though they are essential for good antibody responses.
concepts.question: Why does HIV, which depletes helper T cells, weaken responses to many other infections?

concepts.name: Cytotoxic T cell
concepts.explanation: CD8+ T cells that recognise and kill infected cells, clearing viruses that hide inside cells.
concepts.caveat: Antibody levels get most attention, but T cell responses can protect against severe disease even when antibodies fall.
concepts.question: Why might a vaccine still prevent severe illness after antibody levels have dropped?

concepts.name: B cell
concepts.explanation: Immune cells that make antibodies. When a B cell meets its antigen and gets T cell help, it multiplies and becomes antibody factories.
concepts.caveat: Each B cell recognises one specific shape; the diversity comes from millions of different B cells.
concepts.question: How can the body have B cells ready for viruses it has never seen?

concepts.name: Antibody
concepts.explanation: Y-shaped proteins that bind specific antigens, blocking pathogens from entering cells and marking them for destruction.
concepts.caveat: A high antibody count is not a perfect measure of protection; binding strength and target matter too.
concepts.question: Why might two people with the same antibody level differ in protection?

concepts.name: Germinal center
concepts.explanation: Structures in lymph nodes where B cells mutate and are selected over weeks, producing antibodies that bind more tightly.
concepts.caveat: Because this takes time, antibody quality often keeps improving for weeks or months after vaccination.
concepts.question: Why might spacing two vaccine doses further apart improve the response?

concepts.name: Immunological memory
concepts.explanation: Long-lived memory B and T cells that respond faster and stronger on a second encounter with the same antigen.
concepts.caveat: Memory is not the same as antibodies in the blood; memory can last after antibody levels fall.
concepts.question: If antibodies fade, is someone necessarily unprotected?
phrases: immunological memory B cells T cells

concepts.name: Vaccine
concepts.explanation: A preparation that shows the immune system an antigen safely, so it builds adaptive immunity and memory without the disease.
concepts.caveat: Vaccines differ widely in how long protection lasts and whether they block infection or mainly severe disease.
concepts.question: Why do some vaccines give lifelong protection while others need yearly updates?

concepts.name: Adjuvant
concepts.explanation: An ingredient added to some vaccines to stimulate innate immunity, making the adaptive response stronger.
concepts.caveat: Adjuvants are not preservatives or fillers; their role is to trigger the alarm signals that antigens alone may lack.
concepts.question: Why do purified protein vaccines often need an adjuvant when whole-virus vaccines may not?

concepts.name: mRNA vaccine
concepts.explanation: A vaccine that delivers mRNA instructions in a lipid nanoparticle so your own cells briefly make the antigen protein.
concepts.caveat: The mRNA does not enter the cell nucleus or change DNA, and it is broken down within days.
concepts.question: Why does the body still learn from a protein that was made by its own cells?

concepts.name: Live attenuated vaccine
concepts.explanation: A vaccine using a weakened form of the pathogen that can still replicate a little, often giving strong, long-lasting immunity.
concepts.caveat: They are usually not given to people with weakened immune systems, because the weakened pathogen can still cause illness.
concepts.question: Why might a vaccine that replicates give longer-lasting immunity than one that does not?

concepts.name: Booster dose
concepts.explanation: An extra dose given after the first series to re-activate memory cells, raising antibody levels and often improving their quality.
concepts.caveat: Boosters are needed for some vaccines and not others; "needs a booster" does not mean the vaccine failed.
concepts.question: What is the immune system doing differently on a booster compared with the first dose?

concepts.name: Herd immunity
concepts.explanation: When enough people are immune, a pathogen cannot spread easily, which indirectly protects people who are not immune.
concepts.caveat: The threshold depends on how contagious the pathogen is and whether the vaccine blocks transmission, not just disease.
concepts.question: Why does measles need a much higher vaccination rate for herd immunity than flu?
